name: Which practical questions arise when training an MLP by gradient descent, and which issues of the error surface complicate the descent (local minima, weight space symmetry, saddle points, flat regions, cliffs, local vs. global structure)?
answer:
Practical questions.
Training efficiency: what size of a minibatch? How to choose the learning rate ε(t) and control SGD? How to pre-process the inputs? How to initialize the weights? How to choose the desired output values of the network?
Quality of the resulting model: when to stop training? Regularization techniques. How large a network?
(The lecture illustrates the reasoning on MLP + mse; other topologies and error functions have different but related issues.)

Issues in gradient descent.
• Local minima: small networks have lots of local minima where the descent gets stuck. Recent studies show that for sufficiently large networks all local minima have low values of the error function.
• Model identifiability problem – weight space symmetry: swapping the incoming weights of neurons i and j leaves the same network topology, so many different weight vectors represent the same function.
• Saddle points: one can show (by a combinatorial argument) that larger networks have exponentially more saddle points than local minima.
• Too slow descent – flat regions: the gradient is tiny on plateaus, so the steps are very small.
• Too fast descent – steep cliffs: the gradient is extremely large, and the descent skips important weight vectors (it jumps far away from the region of interest).
• Local vs. global structure: the local shape of the error function may not point towards a good solution. In the lecture's picture the error is flat on the left, rises over a hill and only then drops to a low value on the right; if we initialize on the left, following the local gradient never gets us over the hill to the low-error region.
keyPoints: Efficiency: minibatch size, learning rate, preprocessing, initialization; quality: stopping, regularization, network size
Small networks: many local minima; large networks: local minima have low error
Weight space symmetry (model identifiability)
Saddle points exponentially more frequent than local minima in larger networks
Flat regions → too slow; steep cliffs → huge gradient skips good weights
Local structure may mislead (bad initialization side of a hill)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 112–116 (slides 113–116 contain figures)

name: Roughly, what does the theorem on gradient descent in large networks say? State its assumptions and conclusion.
answer:
Theorem (roughly). Assume:
• activation functions: "smooth" ReLU (softplus) σ(z) = log(1 + exp(z)); in general smooth, non-polynomial, analytic, Lipschitz continuous;
• data: inputs xk of Euclidean norm equal to 1, desired values dk such that all |dk| are bounded by a constant;
• width: the number of hidden neurons per layer is sufficiently large – polynomial in certain numerical characteristics of the inputs (roughly measuring their similarity) and exponential in the depth of the network;
• learning rate: constant and sufficiently small.

Then the gradient descent converges (with high probability w.r.t. the random initialization) to a global minimum with zero error at a linear rate.

Remark: for a special type of network called ResNet (later in the course) the result demands only polynomially many neurons per layer w.r.t. the depth.

Meaning (interpretation, not on the slide): although the error function is non-convex, sufficiently wide (over-parametrised) networks can be trained to zero training error by plain gradient descent – consistent with the observation that large networks do not suffer from bad local minima.
keyPoints: Smooth activations (e.g. softplus log(1 + e^z))
Unit-norm inputs, bounded desired values
Very wide layers: polynomial in data characteristics, exponential in depth
Constant, sufficiently small learning rate
GD converges w.h.p. to a global minimum with zero error at a linear rate
ResNet: only polynomial width in depth needed
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slide 117 (the closing "Meaning" remark is an interpretation)

name: What are the issues in computing the gradient (vanishing/exploding gradients, inexact minibatch gradients), and what considerations determine the choice of the minibatch size?
answer:
Vanishing and exploding gradients. Backpropagation computes
∂Ek/∂yj = yj − dkj for j ∈ Y, and ∂Ek/∂yj = Σr∈j→ ∂Ek/∂yr · σ′r(ξr) · wrj for hidden neurons.
(Explanation, not printed on the slide:) going down through the layers, the derivative is repeatedly multiplied by factors σ′r(ξr) · wrj. If these factors are small, the gradient shrinks towards zero in the lower layers (vanishing); if they are large, it blows up (exploding).

Inexact gradient computation. The minibatch gradient is only an estimate of the true gradient. The standard deviation of the estimate is (roughly) σ/√m, where m is the size of the minibatch and σ is, in the slide's words, the "variance" of the gradient estimate for a single training example (strictly it must be its standard deviation for the formula σ/√m to hold). E.g. minibatch size 10 000 means 100 times more computation than size 100 but gives only 10 times less deviation.

Minibatch size.
• Larger batches provide a more accurate estimate of the gradient, but with less than linear returns.
• Multicore architectures are usually underutilized by extremely small batches.
• If all examples in the batch are processed in parallel (the typical case), the amount of memory scales with the batch size – for many hardware setups this is the limiting factor.
• It is common (especially on GPUs) for power-of-2 batch sizes to offer better runtime; typical sizes range from 32 to 256, with 16 sometimes attempted for large models.
• Small batches can offer a regularizing effect, perhaps due to the noise they add to the learning process. It has been observed in practice that with a larger batch there is a degradation in the quality of the model, as measured by its ability to generalize.
keyPoints: Repeated multiplication by σ′_r(ξ_r) · w_rj → vanishing or exploding gradients
Minibatch gradient is only an estimate of the true gradient
Deviation of the estimate ≈ σ/√m: 100× more computation gives only 10× less deviation
Larger batches: more accurate, less than linear returns, more memory
Powers of 2, typically 32–256
Small batches regularize (noise); large batches generalize worse
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 118–119 (the mechanism of vanishing/exploding gradients and the variance/deviation remark are elaborations)

name: Explain the momentum method: which problem of gradient descent does it address, what is the update formula, and how does SGD with momentum work?
answer:
The issue: in gradient descent, ∇E(w(t)) constantly changes direction (but the error steadily decreases) – in the illustration the descent zig-zags across elongated contours.

Solution: in every step, add the change made in the previous step, weighted by a factor α:
Δw(t) = −ε(t) · Σk∈T ∇Ek(w(t)) + α · Δw(t−1), where 0 < α < 1.

SGD with momentum:
• the weights in w(0) are randomly initialized to values close to 0;
• in step t + 1 (t = 0, 1, 2, …): choose (randomly) a set of training examples T ⊆ {1, …, p} and compute
w(t+1) = w(t) + Δw(t), Δw(t) = −ε(t) · Σk∈T ∇Ek(w(t)) + αΔw(t−1);
• 0 < ε(t) ≤ 1 is the learning rate in step t + 1, 0 < α < 1 measures the "influence" of the momentum, ∇Ek(w(t)) is the gradient of the error of example k.
(The random minibatch is typically implemented by shuffling all data and choosing minibatches sequentially.)

Intuition (a reading of the illustration, not printed on the slides): the update is a decaying sum of past gradients. Components of the gradient that keep changing sign cancel out, while components that consistently point in the same direction accumulate, so the trajectory oscillates less and moves faster along the valley towards the minimum – like a heavy ball rolling downhill.
keyPoints: Problem: the gradient constantly changes direction (zig-zag)
Δw^(t) = −ε(t) Σ_{k∈T} ∇E_k(w^(t)) + α Δw^(t−1)
0 < α < 1 = influence of the momentum
Previous update is added to the current gradient step
Oscillating components cancel, consistent ones accumulate
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 120–122 (slide 121 is a figure; the intuition paragraph interprets it)

name: How does one search for a good learning rate, and what is learning rate scheduling? Demonstrate at least one schedule with its formula.
answer:
Search for the learning rate.
• Use settings from a successful solution of a similar problem as a baseline.
• Search for the learning rate using learning monitoring: search through values from small (e.g. 0.001) to (0.1), possibly multiplying by 2; train for several epochs and observe the learning curves.

Adaptive learning rate (scheduling): instead of a constant ε, the learning rate ε(t) changes with the step t according to a fixed schedule.
• Power scheduling: ε(t) = ε0/(1 + t/s), where ε0 is the initial learning rate and s is a constant number of steps. After s steps the learning rate is ε0/2, after 2s it is ε0/3, etc.
• Exponential scheduling: ε(t) = ε0 · 0.1t/s – the learning rate drops by a factor of 10 every s steps, i.e. it decays faster than in power scheduling.
• Piecewise constant scheduling: a constant learning rate for a number of steps/epochs, then a smaller learning rate, and so on.
• 1cycle scheduling: start by increasing the initial learning rate from ε0 linearly to ε1 (approx. ε1 = 10ε0) halfway through training, then decrease from ε1 linearly back to ε0, and finish by dropping the learning rate by several orders of magnitude (still linearly). According to a 2018 paper by Leslie Smith this may converge much faster.

Why schedule: a large rate at the beginning makes fast progress, a small rate at the end allows settling into a minimum instead of jumping around it.

(For the exam it is enough to understand that there is scheduling and to be able to demonstrate one schedule.)
keyPoints: Baseline from a similar solved problem
Try rates from about 0.001 to 0.1, multiplying by 2; watch learning curves
Power scheduling: ε(t) = ε_0/(1 + t/s)
Exponential scheduling: ε(t) = ε_0 · 0.1^(t/s)
Piecewise constant scheduling
1cycle: linear increase to ε_1 ≈ 10 ε_0, linear decrease, final drop

name: Explain AdaGrad: the motivation, the complete update formulas and the meaning of the constants. What is its main disadvantage?
answer:
Motivation. Fixed schedules use the same learning rate for all weights. It is better to have
• larger rates for weights with smaller updates,
• smaller rates for weights with larger updates.
AdaGrad uses individually adapting learning rates for each weight.

SGD with AdaGrad.
• The weights in w(0) are randomly initialized to values close to 0.
• In step t + 1 (t = 0, 1, 2, …): choose (randomly) a minibatch T ⊆ {1, …, p} and compute
wji(t+1) = wji(t) + Δwji(t), where
Δwji(t) = − η / √(rji(t) + δ) · Σk∈T ∂Ek/∂wji(w(t))
and
rji(t) = rji(t−1) + ( Σk∈T ∂Ek/∂wji(w(t)) )2.
• η is a constant expressing the influence of the learning rate, typically 0.01.
• δ > 0 is a smoothing term (typically 1e-8) avoiding division by 0.

How it works: rji accumulates the squares of all past (minibatch) partial derivatives w.r.t. the weight wji. A weight with large gradients gets a large rji and hence a small effective rate η/√(rji + δ); a weight with small gradients keeps a larger rate.

Main disadvantage: the gradients are accumulated throughout the whole learning process, so rji only grows and the effective learning rates only shrink. If the learning needs to get over several "hills" before settling in a deep "valley", the weight updates get far too small before getting to it.
keyPoints: Individual learning rate for every weight
Larger rates for weights with small updates, smaller for large updates
Δw_ji = −η/√(r_ji + δ) · Σ_{k∈T} ∂E_k/∂w_ji
r_ji^(t) = r_ji^(t−1) + (Σ_{k∈T} ∂E_k/∂w_ji)²
η ≈ 0.01; δ ≈ 1e-8 avoids division by zero
Disadvantage: accumulation over the whole history → updates become too small

name: Explain RMSProp: how does it fix the disadvantage of AdaGrad, what are its update formulas, and what does the lecture say about other optimization methods and the choice among them?
answer:
Idea. The main disadvantage of AdaGrad is the accumulation of gradients throughout the learning process. RMSProp uses an exponentially decaying average to discard history from the extreme past, so that it can converge rapidly after finding a convex bowl – as if it were an instance of AdaGrad initialized within that bowl.

SGD with RMSProp.
• The weights in w(0) are randomly initialized to values close to 0.
• In step t + 1: choose (randomly) a minibatch T ⊆ {1, …, p} and compute
wji(t+1) = wji(t) + Δwji(t), where
Δwji(t) = − η / √(rji(t) + δ) · Σk∈T ∂Ek/∂wji(w(t))
and
rji(t) = ρ · rji(t−1) + (1 − ρ) · ( Σk∈T ∂Ek/∂wji(w(t)) )2.
• η is a constant expressing the influence of the learning rate (Hinton suggests ρ = 0.9 and η = 0.001).
• δ > 0 is a smoothing term (typically 1e-8) avoiding division by 0.
The only difference from AdaGrad is the factor ρ: old squared gradients are multiplied by ρ in every step and thus forgotten exponentially fast, so rji does not grow without bound.

Other methods and the choice. There are more methods, such as AdaDelta and Adam (RMSProp combined with momentum). Which algorithm should one choose? Unfortunately there is currently no consensus. According to a study, the family of algorithms with adaptive learning rates (represented by RMSProp and AdaDelta) performed fairly robustly, but no single best algorithm has emerged. The most popular algorithms actively in use include SGD, SGD with momentum, RMSProp, RMSProp with momentum, AdaDelta and Adam; the choice seems to depend largely on the user's familiarity with the algorithm.
keyPoints: Exponentially decaying average discards the distant history
r_ji^(t) = ρ r_ji^(t−1) + (1 − ρ)(Σ_{k∈T} ∂E_k/∂w_ji)²
Δw_ji = −η/√(r_ji + δ) · Σ_{k∈T} ∂E_k/∂w_ji
Adam = RMSProp combined with momentum
No consensus on the best optimizer; adaptive methods are fairly robust

name: What generic requirements are imposed on (hidden) activation functions, and why and how are inputs preprocessed before training?
answer:
Generic requirements on activation functions:
1. Differentiability – to do gradient descent.
2. Non-linearity – linear multi-layer networks are equivalent to single-layer ones.
3. Monotonicity – local extrema of activation functions induce local extrema of the error function.
4. "Linearity" – preserve as much linearity as possible; linear models are easiest to fit; find the "minimum" non-linearity needed to solve the given task.
The choice of activation functions is closely related to input preprocessing and the initial choice of weights.

Input preprocessing.
• Some inputs may be much larger than others – e.g. the height vs. the weight of a person, the maximum speed of a car (in km/h) vs. its price (in CZK).
• Large inputs have a greater influence on the training than the small ones. Also, too large inputs may slow down learning (saturation of some activation functions).
• Typical standardization (per input component): average = 0 (subtract the mean) and variance = 1 (divide by the standard deviation). The mean and the standard deviation may be estimated from the data (the training set).
keyPoints: Differentiability (needed for gradient descent)
Non-linearity (linear multilayer nets collapse to a single layer)
Monotonicity (extrema of σ induce extrema of the error)
"Linearity": as close to linear as the task allows
Inputs of different scales: large ones dominate and may saturate activations
Standardize: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation (estimated on the training set)

name: Explain the intuition behind weight initialization and derive the normal LeCun initialization, including the proof that Var[ξ] = n · w<sup>2</sup>.
answer:
Intuition. Assume the weights are chosen randomly – from what distribution? Consider the behaviour of a deep network: small weights make the values of inner potentials vanish, large weights make them explode. Hence we want to choose the weights so that the inner potentials of neurons are stable (similar in all layers of the network).

Normal LeCun initialization. Assume the input data have mean 0 and variance 1. Consider a neuron j from the first layer with n inputs, and assume its weights are chosen randomly from the normal distribution N(0, w2), all random choices being independent.
The rule: choose the standard deviation w of the weights so that the standard deviation oj of ξj satisfies oj ≈ 1.
Basic properties of the variance of independent variables give oj = √n · w. Thus by putting w = √(1/n) we obtain oj = 1. The same works for higher layers; n then corresponds to the number of neurons in the layer one level lower. This gives
wi ∼ N(0, 1/n).

Derivation. Consider a single neuron without bias with inner potential ξ = Σi=1..n wixi. Consider all wi and xi as independent random variables (so ξ is also a random variable), where
• wi ∼ N(0, w2) for i = 1, …, n, w a constant,
• E[xi] = 0 and Var[xi] = E[(xi − E xi)2] = 1.
We prove Var[ξ] = n · w2:
1. E[ξ] = E[Σ wixi] = Σ E[wixi] = (independence) Σ E[wi]E[xi] = 0.
2. Var[wixi] = E[wi2xi2] − E[wixi]2 = (independence) E[wi2]E[xi2] − 0 = w2 · 1 = w2, because E[wi2] = Var[wi] = w2 and E[xi2] = Var[xi] = 1 (both have zero mean).
3. Var[ξ] = Var[Σ wixi] = (independence) Σ Var[wixi] = Σi=1..n w2 = n · w2.
Therefore the standard deviation of ξ is √n · w, and requiring it to be 1 gives w2 = 1/n.
keyPoints: Small weights → potentials vanish; large weights → potentials explode; want stable potentials
Inputs standardized (mean 0, variance 1); weights ∼ N(0, w²), independent
E[ξ] = 0 by independence
Var[w_i x_i] = E[w_i²]E[x_i²] = w²
Var[ξ] = n·w² → o_j = √n · w; set w = √(1/n)
Normal LeCun: w_i ∼ N(0, 1/n), n = number of inputs of the neuron

name: Describe the Glorot (Xavier) initialization in the normal and uniform versions and the uniform LeCun initialization. What does Glorot initialization add to LeCun's reasoning?
answer:
Normal Glorot initialization. The LeCun heuristic ignores the variance of the gradient – it is concerned only with the "size" of activations in the forward pass. Glorot & Bengio (2010) presented a normalized initialization choosing the weights randomly from
N(0, 2/(m + n)) = N(0, 1/((m + n)/2)),
where n is the number of inputs to the layer and m is the number of neurons in the layer above. It is designed as a compromise between the goal of initializing all layers to have the same activation variance and the goal of initializing all layers to have the same gradient variance. This gives the normal Glorot (normal Xavier) initialization: wi ∼ N(0, 2/(m + n)).

Uniform LeCun initialization. Assume the input data have mean 0 and variance 1. Consider a neuron j from the first layer with n inputs, with weights chosen randomly from the uniform distribution U(−w, w), all choices independent. As before we want the standard deviation oj of the inner potential ξj to be approximately 1. Basic properties of the variance of independent variables give oj = √(n/3) · w (the variance of U(−w, w) is w2/3). Thus by putting w = √(3/n) we obtain oj = 1:
wi ∼ U(−√(3/n), √(3/n)).

Uniform Glorot initialization. Similarly to the normal case, we normalize the initialization w.r.t. both the forward and the backward pass:
wi ∼ U(−√(6/(m + n)), √(6/(m + n))) = U(−√(3/((m + n)/2)), √(3/((m + n)/2))),
i.e. the uniform LeCun formula with n replaced by the average (m + n)/2 of the numbers of inputs and of neurons in the layer above.
keyPoints: LeCun considers only forward-pass activation variance
Glorot: compromise between equal activation variance and equal gradient variance
Normal Glorot: w_i ∼ N(0, 2/(m + n)), n inputs, m neurons in the layer above
Uniform LeCun: o_j = √(n/3)·w → w_i ∼ U(−√(3/n), √(3/n))
Uniform Glorot: w_i ∼ U(−√(6/(m + n)), √(6/(m + n)))
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 136–138 (the variance w²/3 of U(−w, w) is the standard fact behind the slide's formula)

name: Characterise ReLU and at least one of its modern variants as hidden activation functions, explain why LeCun initialization is not justified for ReLU and what He initialization does instead, and say how initialization methods are matched to activations.
answer:
ReLU. For hidden neurons, sigmoidal functions are often substituted with piece-wise linear activations; the most prominent is ReLU, σ(ξ) = max{0, ξ}.
• THE default activation function recommended for most feedforward neural networks.
• As close to a linear function as possible; very simple; does not saturate for large potentials.
• Dead for negative potentials (zero output and zero gradient).

Variants (one is enough for the exam).
• Leaky ReLU: generalizes ReLU with a small slope for negative potentials, so it is not dead there; experimentally not much better than ReLU.
• ELU ("smoothed" ReLU): σ(ξ) = α(exp(ξ) − 1) for ξ < 0 and σ(ξ) = ξ for ξ ≥ 0, where α is a parameter; ELU converges to −α as ξ → −∞. As opposed to ReLU: smooth, always non-zero gradient (but saturates), slower to compute.
• SELU: a scaled variant of ELU, σ(ξ) = λ · ELU(ξ). It is self-normalizing: the output of each layer tends to preserve mean (close to) 0 and standard deviation (close to) 1 for λ ≈ 1.050 and α ≈ 1.673, properly initialized weights and normalized inputs.

Normal He initialization.
• ReLU is not as sensitive to a large variance of the inner potential as sigmoidal functions, but it is still good to keep the variance constant (at least due to the output layer).
• LeCun initialization cannot be justified for ReLU: ReLU is not a symmetric function, so even if the inner potential ξj has variance 1, this is not true of the output – the variance is halved.
• Modifying the normal LeCun initialization to take the halving into account gives wi ∼ N(0, 2/n) (LeCun is N(0, 1/n)).

Matching initialization to activation (n = number of inputs to the layer, m = number of neurons in the layer): there is an assignment of initialization methods to activation functions – normal Glorot N(0, 2/(m + n)) is suitable for none (linear), tanh, logistic, softmax; normal He N(0, 2/n) for ReLU and leaky ReLU; normal LeCun N(0, 1/n) for SELU. (The exact table need not be memorised.)

Choosing the hidden activation: the default is ReLU; according to A. Géron: SELU > ELU > leaky ReLU > ReLU > tanh > logistic.
keyPoints: ReLU max{0, ξ}: default, nearly linear, no saturation for large potentials, dead for negative ones
One variant, e.g. ELU: α(e^ξ − 1) for ξ < 0, ξ otherwise (or leaky ReLU / SELU)
ReLU is not symmetric → output variance is halved → LeCun not justified
Normal He: w_i ∼ N(0, 2/n)
Initialization is matched to the activation (Glorot: tanh/logistic; He: ReLU; LeCun: SELU)
Default choice is ReLU
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 139–144 (slide 142 is a plot of ELU, LReLU, ReLU, SReLU)

name: Explain batch normalization as presented ("roughly"): the intuition, the computation during training with formulas, the trainable parameters, and what is done during inference.
answer:
Intuition. Instead of keeping mean = 0 and variance = 1 only implicitly through a clever weight initialization, we may renormalize the values of neurons throughout the layers. The output values of the neurons in the ℓ-th layer can be seen as inputs to the sub-network consisting of all layers above the ℓ-th one – so standardize the values of the ℓ-th layer just as we did with the input data. For this we need a "dataset" of values of the ℓ-th layer; a (mini)batch provides it.

Training. Consider the ℓ-th layer with n neurons and a batch of training examples {(xk, dk) | k = 1, …, p} (typically a minibatch).
1. For every k = 1, …, p compute the values of the neurons in the ℓ-th layer for the input xk and obtain a vector zk = (zk1, …, zkn).
2. Normalize every component over the batch to mean 0 and variance 1, obtaining ẑ1, …, ẑp:
ẑki = (zki − μi) / si, where μi = (1/p) Σk=1..p zki and si = √( (1/p) Σk=1..p (zki − μi)2 ).
3. For every k give γ · ẑk + δ (component-wise) as the output of the ℓ-th layer instead of zk. Here γ and δ are new trainable weights (vectors), so the network can learn the scale and shift that suit it best.

Inference. During inference we have just a single value z of the layer ℓ for an input x, so there is no batch to compute statistics from; we use μi and si estimated on a population (e.g. a larger sample of the training set).
keyPoints: Explicitly renormalize layer values instead of relying on initialization
Layer ℓ outputs are inputs of the sub-network above it
Per neuron i over the batch: μ_i mean, s_i standard deviation, ẑ_ki = (z_ki − μ_i)/s_i
Layer outputs γ·ẑ_k + δ with trainable γ and δ
Inference: μ_i and s_i estimated on a population (larger sample of the training set)

name: What is generalization and why is regularization "a big issue" in neural networks? Explain early stopping, including the data split and the possible stopping rules.
answer:
Generalization = the ability to cope with new, unseen instances. Data are mostly noisy, so it is not a good idea to fit them exactly; in function approximation the network should not return exactly the results from the training set. More formally, it is typically assumed that the training set has been generated as
dkj = gj(xk) + Θkj,
where gj is the "underlying" function corresponding to the output neuron j ∈ Y and Θkj is random noise. The network should fit gj, not the noise. Methods improving generalization are called regularization methods.

Why a big issue: neural networks typically use a huge number of parameters and are thus very susceptible to overfitting (von Neumann: "With four parameters, I can fit an elephant, and with five, I can make him wiggle his trunk.").

Early stopping means that we stop learning before it reaches a minimum of the error E. Reasons:
• in many applications the error function is not the main thing we want to optimize (e.g. a trading system should maximize profit, not minimize a strange error function designed to be easily differentiable);
• minimizing E completely is not good for generalization.
Standard approach: train on one set and stop on another one. Divide the dataset into
• a training set (e.g. 60 %) – train the network here,
• a validation set (e.g. 20 %) – use it to stop the training,
• a test set (e.g. 20 %) – use it to evaluate the final model.

Stopping rules:
• observe E (or any other function of interest) on the validation set; if it does not improve for the last k steps, stop;
• alternatively, observe the gradient; if it is small for some time, stop. (Some studies have shown that this traditional rule is not too good – the gradient may be larger close to minimum values; on the other hand, E does not have to be evaluated, which saves time.)
To compare models one may use ML techniques such as various types of cross-validation.
keyPoints: Generalization = coping with unseen instances; fit g_j, not the noise (d_kj = g_j(x_k) + Θ_kj)
Many parameters → overfitting; regularization = methods improving generalization
Early stopping: stop before reaching the minimum of E
Training / validation / test sets (e.g. 60/20/20)
Stop when validation error has not improved for k steps
Alternative: stop on a small gradient (cheaper but less reliable)
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 149–150 and 153–155 (elephant slides 151–152 omitted)

name: How should the size of a network be chosen, and what does the "feature extraction" example (network 64-2-3) illustrate?
answer:
Size of the network – a similar problem as with the training duration:
• a too small network is not able to capture the intrinsic properties of the training set (underfitting);
• large networks overfit faster.
"Solution": the optimal number of neurons – but
• there are some (useless) theoretical bounds;
• there are algorithms dynamically adding/removing neurons (not much used nowadays);
• in practice: start with an existing network solving a similar problem. If you are truly desperate, trying to solve a brand new problem, you may try an ancient rule of thumb: the number of neurons ≈ ten times less than the number of training instances.
• Experiment, experiment, experiment.

Feature extraction. Consider a two-layer network. The hidden neurons are supposed to represent "patterns" in the inputs. Example: a network 64-2-3 for letter classification – 64 inputs (8 × 8 pixel images of noisy letters E, L, F), only 2 hidden neurons, 3 outputs (one per letter). The figure shows the learned input-to-hidden weights of the two hidden neurons drawn as 8 × 8 images: each highlights the strokes that distinguish the letters (e.g. the horizontal bars by which E, F and L differ). The two hidden neurons thus extract the features sufficient for the output layer to tell the three classes apart – the hidden layer learns a compressed, task-relevant representation of the input.
keyPoints: Too small: cannot capture the properties of the training set
Too large: overfits faster
Theoretical bounds are useless; dynamic adding/removing of neurons is not used much
Practice: start from an existing network for a similar problem and experiment
Rule of thumb: neurons ≈ training instances / 10
Hidden neurons represent patterns (features) of the inputs – 64-2-3 letter example
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slides 156–157 (slide 157 is a figure; the reading of the weight images interprets it)

name: Explain ensemble methods and bagging, and then dropout: the algorithm, its formal description via inner potentials, its relation to bagging, and what happens during inference.
answer:
Ensemble methods are techniques for reducing the generalization error by combining several models. They work because different models will usually not make all the same errors on the test set. Idea: train several different models separately, then have all of the models vote on the output for test examples.

Bagging:
• generate k training sets T1, …, Tk by sampling from T uniformly with replacement (if the number of samples is |T|, then on average |Ti| = (1 − 1/e)|T| distinct examples);
• for each i, train a model Mi on Ti;
• combine the outputs of the models: for regression by averaging, for classification by (majority) voting.

Dropout – the algorithm. In every step of the gradient descent:
• choose randomly a set N of neurons, each neuron being included independently with probability 1/2 (in practice, different probabilities are used as well);
• do the forward and backward propagations only using the selected neurons (i.e. leave the weights of the other neurons unchanged).

Formally. Without dropout: ξj = Σi∈j← wjiyi. With dropout: draw ri ∼ Bernoulli(1/2) for all i ∈ j← ∖ {0} and use
ξj = Σi∈j← wji(riyi)
(randomly chosen neurons are masked out; the formal unit input 0 is never dropped).

Relation to bagging. Dropout resembles bagging: a large ensemble of neural networks is trained "at once" on parts of the data. It is not exactly the same: the models share parameters, each model inheriting a different subset of parameters from the parent network. This parameter sharing makes it possible to represent an exponential number of models with a tractable amount of memory. In bagging each model is trained to convergence on its own training set, which would be infeasible for large networks/training sets.

Inference. Do not drop out neurons and multiply the values of neurons by 1/2. This compensates for the fact that without dropout there are twice as many (active) neurons contributing to each potential.
keyPoints: Ensembles: different models make different errors; combine by averaging/voting
Bagging: k sets sampled with replacement, one model per set
Dropout: in every step keep each neuron with probability 1/2, propagate only through kept neurons
ξ_j = Σ w_ji (r_i y_i), r_i ∼ Bernoulli(1/2)
Like bagging, but exponentially many sub-models share parameters
Inference: no dropping, multiply neuron values by 1/2

name: Explain weight decay and L2 regularization, and prove that weight decay is equivalent to gradient descent (with a constant learning rate) on an error function with an L2 penalty.
answer:
Idea. Generalization can be improved by removing "unimportant" weights. Penalising large weights gives a stronger indication about their importance.

Weight decay. In every step we decrease the weights (multiplicatively):
wji(t+1) = (1 − ζ) · wji(t) − ε · ∂E/∂wji(w(t)).
Intuition: unimportant weights will be pushed to 0, important weights will survive the decay (because the gradient term keeps restoring them).

Equivalence. Weight decay is equivalent to gradient descent with a constant learning rate ε and the error function
E′(w) = E(w) + (ζ/(2ε)) · (w · w),
where (ζ/(2ε))(w · w) is the L2 regularization term that penalizes large weights (w · w = Σ wji2).

Proof. Differentiate E′ w.r.t. a weight wji:
∂E′/∂wji = ∂E/∂wji + (ζ/(2ε)) · 2wji = ∂E/∂wji + (ζ/ε) · wji.
A gradient descent step on E′ with learning rate ε gives
wji(t+1) = wji(t) − ε · ∂E′/∂wji(w(t)) = wji(t) − ε · ∂E/∂wji(w(t)) − ζ · wji(t) = (1 − ζ) · wji(t) − ε · ∂E/∂wji(w(t)),
which is exactly the weight decay update. □

Remark. Gradient descent with a constant learning rate is used only to illustrate the equivalence between L2 regularization and weight decay; both methods can be combined with other learning algorithms (AdaGrad, etc.).
keyPoints: Remove unimportant weights by penalising large weights
Weight decay: w^(t+1) = (1 − ζ) w^(t) − ε ∂E/∂w
Equivalent error: E′(w) = E(w) + (ζ/(2ε)) (w·w)
∂E′/∂w_ji = ∂E/∂w_ji + (ζ/ε) w_ji
GD step on E′ with rate ε reproduces the decay factor (1 − ζ)
Both can be combined with other optimizers
source: PV021 L4 (inferred boundary), OLD_lecture_slides_HANDOUT-2025.pdf, slide 161 (the differentiation step spells out the stated equivalence)
